module_title: Getting Started: The Car Breaking & Scrapyard Business

lessons.title: Understanding the car breaking and metal scrapyard value chain in Africa
lessons.body:
The car breaking and metal scrapyard business in Africa is a cashâflow industry built on recovering value from old vehicles and scrap metal. The value chain starts with sourcing: you buy endâofâlife cars from individuals, insurance companies, taxi fleets, or government auctions. In many African cities, a nonârunning sedan might cost $200â$500, while a small truck could be $800â$1,500. You then tow or drive it to your yard.

Next comes dismantling. You remove usable parts: alternators, starters, radiators, batteries, tyres, and engines. These are cleaned, tested, and sold to mechanics or roadside parts dealers. A used alternator for a Toyota Corolla might sell for $25â$40, while a good engine can fetch $300â$800. Parts that donât sell are sorted by metal type: steel, aluminium, copper, and brass. Copper wiring, for example, sells for $2â$4 per kilogram to local foundries or exporters.

The final stage is processing and selling scrap metal. You cut large pieces with a hacksaw or angle grinder, then sell to larger scrap dealers or directly to steel mills. In countries like Nigeria, Kenya, or South Africa, a tonne of mixed steel scrap might earn $150â$300. Aluminium cans and castings can bring $800â$1,200 per tonne. The key is to separate metals carefullyâcontaminated loads get lower prices.

This business is labourâintensive but lowâtech. You can start with a hand truck, a set of spanners, and a hacksaw. The value chain works because Africa has a growing vehicle population, limited recycling infrastructure, and high demand for affordable spare parts. By understanding each stepâsourcing, dismantling, sorting, and sellingâyou can turn a dead car into a steady income stream.

lessons.title: Legal requirements and permits for starting a scrapyard in your country
lessons.body:
Before you open a scrapyard, you must comply with local laws. In most African countries, you need a business registration certificate from the companies commission. For a sole proprietorship, this costs about $20â$50 in Kenya, Nigeria, or Ghana. You also need a tax identification number (TIN) and a local government trade licence, which can cost $50â$200 per year depending on your municipality.

Environmental permits are critical. Scrapyards can leak oil, battery acid, and coolant. In South Africa, you must register with the Department of Environmental Affairs and get a waste management licence. In Kenya, the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) requires an environmental impact assessment (EIA) for yards above a certain size. The EIA can cost $300â$1,000. Even for small yards, you must have a plan for used oil, tyres, and batteries. Many countries ban open burning of cables to recover copperâyou can be fined heavily.

You also need a scrap metal dealerâs licence. In Nigeria, the Scrap Metal Dealers Association requires registration, and some states demand a police clearance certificate to prove you are not dealing in stolen vehicles. In Uganda, you must get a permit from the Ministry of Trade. Always keep receipts for every car you buy, including the sellerâs ID copy and vehicle registration papers. This protects you if police question the origin of a vehicle.

Finally, check zoning laws. You cannot operate a noisy, dusty scrapyard in a residential area. Look for land zoned for industrial or commercial use. If you rent, get a written lease. Visit your local council, environmental office, and police station to ask exactly what is needed. Budget $200â$800 for all permits in the first year. Cutting corners leads to closures, fines, or confiscation of your stock.

lessons.title: Choosing a strategic location: near roads, towns, or industrial areas
lessons.body:
Location can make or break your scrapyard. You need a site that is easy to reach for both sellers and buyers. The best spots are on the outskirts of a town, along a major road or highway. Why? Because tow trucks and customers bringing scrap donât want to drive deep into traffic. A yard 5â10 km from the city centre on a tarmac road is ideal. In Accra, for example, yards along the Nsawam Road do well because they are visible and accessible.

You also need spaceâat least half an acre (2,000 square metres) to start. The ground should be flat, wellâdrained, and preferably with a hard surface like compacted gravel or concrete. Muddy yards lose metal in the mud and are hard to work in during rains. If you can, choose a site near an industrial area where factories generate scrap metal and also buy your sorted materials. Being close to a steel mill or foundry saves transport costs.

Consider neighbours. You will make noise with hammers, grinders, and trucks. You will have dust and occasional oil spills. So keep away from schools, hospitals, and dense housing. A site near a mechanic village or auto repair cluster is excellent because those businesses both supply old cars and buy spare parts. In Lagos, the Ladipo market area is a hub for used partsâa yard nearby has ready customers.

Check access to utilities: water for cleaning parts, electricity for tools (or a generator), and phone network for calls. Security is also keyâscrap metal is valuable and can be stolen. A fenced yard with a gate and a night watchman is worth the extra cost. Finally, verify land ownership or lease terms. A verbal agreement can lead to eviction. Get a written lease of at least 3â5 years so you can build your business without moving.

lessons.title: Essential tools and equipment for a beginner car breaker
lessons.body:
You donât need a fortune to start breaking cars. Begin with a basic set of hand tools: a socket set (8mmâ24mm), combination spanners, screwdrivers (flat and Phillips), pliers, a hammer, and a chisel. A good socket set costs $30â$60. You also need a hacksaw with spare blades for cutting metal, and a heavyâduty pry bar to separate panels. A wheel brace and jack are essential for removing wheels and tyres.

For dismantling engines and transmissions, youâll need a torque wrench (to avoid overâtightening bolts), a breaker bar, and an engine hoist or a strong chain block. A used engine hoist can cost $150â$300. If you canât afford one, use a sturdy tree branch or a steel Aâframe with a chain blockâjust make sure itâs safe. You also need drain pans for oil, coolant, and fuel. Never drain these onto the ground.

Power tools speed up work. An angle grinder with cutting and grinding discs ($40â$80) is the most versatile tool for cutting exhausts, chassis, and seized bolts. A reciprocating saw ($60â$120) is great for cutting through car bodies. A cordless drill/driver ($50â$100) helps with removing panels. If you have electricity, a small air compressor ($100â$200) and impact wrench make removing rusty bolts much easier. A generator ($200â$400) is useful if your yard has no power.

For moving heavy parts, a hand truck (trolley) and a wheelbarrow are cheap and essential. A magnetic pickâup tool saves dropped nuts. For safety, you need a fire extinguisher, a firstâaid kit, and a spill kit (sand or sawdust for oil). Finally, a small welding machine ($150â$300) lets you cut and repair metal for resale. Start with the basics, then reinvest profits into better tools.

lessons.title: Safety gear and basic first aid for scrapyard work
lessons.body:
Scrapyard work is dangerous: sharp metal, heavy parts, toxic fluids, and fire risks. You must wear personal protective equipment (PPE) every day. Start with steelâtoe safety boots ($20â$40). They protect your feet from falling parts and nails. Never wear sandals or open shoes. Next, heavyâduty work gloves ($5â$15) to prevent cuts and burns. Keep a spare pair. Safety glasses ($3â$10) are essential when grinding, cutting, or hammeringâflying metal can blind you.

Hearing protection (earplugs or earmuffs, $5â$20) is needed when using grinders or hammers. A dust mask or respirator ($10â$30) protects you from brake dust, paint, and rust particles. When draining fuel or working with batteries, wear chemicalâresistant gloves and a face shield. Always have a fire extinguisher (dry powder, $30â$60) and a bucket of sand near your work area. Never smoke or use open flames near fuel tanks or batteries.

Basic first aid can save a life. Keep a firstâaid kit ($20â$40) stocked with bandages, antiseptic cream, gauze, adhesive tape, scissors, and painkillers. For cuts, clean the wound with clean water, apply antiseptic, and cover with a sterile bandage. If bleeding is heavy, apply pressure and seek medical help. For burns, cool the area with running water for 10 minutes, then cover loosely. For eye injuries, flush with clean water and go to a clinic immediately.

You must also handle hazardous fluids safely. Drain oil, coolant, and brake fluid into labelled containers. Never mix them. Used oil can be sold to recyclers. Battery acid is corrosiveâwear goggles and gloves, and neutralise spills with baking soda. Keep a written emergency plan: phone numbers for a clinic, fire service, and a trusted neighbour. Train anyone working with you on these rules. A safe yard is a productive yard.

lessons.title: Setting up a simple record-keeping system for purchases and sales
lessons.body:
Record keeping is the difference between a hobby and a real business. You need to know what you bought, what you sold, and what you still have. Start with a simple cash bookâa notebook with columns for date, description, money in, and money out. Every time you buy a car, write the date, sellerâs name, vehicle make and model, registration number, and amount paid. Keep a copy of the sellerâs ID and the vehicle papers. This protects you from stolenâgoods accusations.

For sales, record the date, item sold (e.g., âalternator for Toyota Hiluxâ), buyerâs name, and price. If you sell scrap metal by weight, note the weight and price per kilogram. At the end of each week, total your income and expenses. This tells you if you are making a profit. A simple exercise book costs $1â$2. You can also use a free spreadsheet app on your phone, like Google Sheets, if you have a smartphone.

Inventory is critical. Make a list of all major parts you have in stock: engines, gearboxes, alternators, starters, radiators, batteries, tyres. Write the date you removed them and a condition note (e.g., âtested, goodâ). Update the list when you sell. This prevents theft and helps you answer customers quickly. For scrap metal, keep separate piles for steel, aluminium, copper, and brass. Weigh each pile monthly and record the weights.

Finally, keep receipts for all expenses: tools, fuel, transport, permits, and wages. At tax time, these reduce your taxable profit. If you have employees, keep a simple wage book. Review your records every month. Are you spending too much on transport? Are certain parts not selling? Adjust your buying. Good records turn guesswork into decisions. Start today with a notebook and a penâno excuses.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Setting Up Your Car Breaking & Metal Scrapyard Business in Africa

This lesson is your working manual. It pulls together the legal, physical, and financial fundamentals you need to move from "I want to start a scrapyard" to "I am buying my first end-of-life vehicle (ELV) and selling sorted metal." Everything here is written for the African operating environment â where informal supply chains, cash transactions, and weak enforcement are the norm, and where the smart operator wins by being organised, legal, and trusted.

Read it once. Then use the tables, the checklist, and the diagram as daily tools.

1. The Value Chain You Are Entering

Car breaking is not "collecting scrap." It is a disassembly and materials-recovery business. The value chain in most African markets runs like this:

Source â Transport â Assessment â Depollution â Dismantling â Sorting â Sale/Export

At each stage you either add value or lose money. The operators who make real margins are those who separate materials early and sell to the highest-value buyer at each point â not those who dump everything into one pile and sell by weight to the first dealer who arrives.

2. Legal Requirements and Permits

Requirements vary by country, but the pattern across Africa is consistent. You will typically need a mix of business registration, environmental authorisation, and local government approval. Do not skip these â unlicensed yards are the first to be shut down when enforcement sweeps happen, and you cannot export or invoice formal buyers without papers.

Table 1: Common Legal & Permit Requirements for a Scrapyard in Selected African Countries
Country Business Registration Environmental Permit Local / Trade Approval
Kenya eCitizen business name / company (Registrar of Companies) NEMA EIA licence (Environmental Management & Co-ordination Act) County single business permit; scrap metal dealer licence (Scrap Metal Act 2015)
Nigeria CAC registration (Corporate Affairs Commission) NESREA permit; state environmental agency clearance Local Government trade permit; scrap dealers association registration
South Africa CIPC company registration National Environmental Management Act (NEMA) authorisation; waste licence Municipal business licence; Second-Hand Goods Act registration (SAPS)
Ghana Registrar General's Department EPA Ghana permit (Environmental Protection Agency Act) MMDA business operating permit; scrap dealers registration
Uganda URSB business registration NEMA licence; waste management permit KCCA / district trade licence

Sources: Kenya NEMA (2023); Nigeria NESREA (2022); South Africa DFFE (2023); Ghana EPA (2022); Uganda NEMA (2023). Always confirm current fees and forms with the relevant authority â regulations change.

â ï¸ SAFETY & LEGAL WARNING

Never accept a vehicle without a proof of ownership (logbook, deregistration certificate, or police clearance). Buying stolen vehicles â even unknowingly â is a criminal offence in every African jurisdiction and will result in confiscation, fines, and possible imprisonment. Also: never drain fuel, oil, or refrigerant into the ground or a storm drain. These fluids are hazardous waste; improper disposal carries heavy environmental penalties and contaminates your own site. Store all fluids in labelled, sealed containers and use a licensed disposal contractor.

3. Choosing a Strategic Location

Location determines your transport cost, your customer base, and your regulatory risk. The best sites balance three factors:

  • Proximity to supply: Near major roads, taxi ranks, industrial areas, or insurance salvage yards. Every kilometre you tow an ELV costs money.
  • Proximity to buyers: Near mechanics, panel beaters, foundries, or metal dealers who will buy your sorted output.
  • Zoning and neighbours: Industrial or commercial zoning. Residential areas will generate complaints about noise, dust, and traffic â and complaints trigger inspections.

A site on the edge of a town, on a feeder road to an industrial zone, with space for a weighbridge and a hard standing area, is close to ideal. Avoid flood-prone land â contaminated runoff is an environmental liability and a health risk to your workers.

4. Essential Tools and Equipment for a Beginner

You do not need a fortune to start. You need the right core tools, and you add specialised equipment as revenue grows. The table below lists the beginner essentials with indicative costs in USD (2024 estimates, East/West Africa).

Table 2: Beginner Tool & Equipment Checklist with Indicative Costs
Item Purpose Indicative Cost (USD) Priority
Angle grinder + cutting discs Cutting bolts, exhausts, body panels 60 â 120 Essential
Socket & spanner set (metric) Dismantling engines, suspension, interiors 80 â 200 Essential
Hydraulic jack + axle stands Lifting vehicles safely for under-body work 100 â 250 Essential
Engine crane / hoist Removing engines and gearboxes 200 â 500 High
Fluid drain pans + storage drums Capturing oil, coolant, fuel, brake fluid 50 â 150 Essential
Battery handling trolley Moving lead-acid batteries safely 80 â 200 High
Weighing scale (platform or crane) Accurate metal sales; fair pricing 150 â 600 High
Hand truck / pallet jack Moving parts and sorted metal 60 â 180 Medium
Shelving / racking Organised parts storage; inventory control 100 â 400 Medium

Sources: Indicative market prices compiled from regional tool suppliers and scrapyard operator interviews (Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, 2024). Prices vary by country and import duty.

5. Safety Gear and Basic First Aid

Scrapyard work is dangerous. Cuts, crush injuries, burns, and chemical exposure are common. The minimum safety kit for every worker:

  • Safety boots (steel toe, puncture-resistant sole)
  • Heavy-duty gloves (cut-resistant for handling metal; chemical-resistant for fluids)
  • Safety glasses / face shield (grinding, cutting, battery work)
  • Ear protection (grinders, hammering)
  • High-visibility vest (vehicle movement on site)
  • First aid kit â burns, cuts, eye wash, and a written emergency contact list

Train every worker on safe lifting, fuel handling, and battery acid first aid. A 30-minute induction prevents most injuries. Keep a first aid kit in a fixed, marked location and check it monthly.

6. Simple Record-Keeping for Purchases and Sales

You cannot grow a business you cannot measure. A simple record system â even a notebook and a phone â will transform your margins. Record every transaction with:

  • Date and vehicle/description
  • Source (seller name, ID, vehicle registration)
  • Purchase price and transport cost
  • Parts removed and their sale price
  • Metal sold (kg, grade, price per kg, buyer)
  • Daily cash balance

A simple spreadsheet or a free app like Wave or Kobo Collect works well. The key is consistency â record the same day, every day. After one month you will know which vehicles are profitable and which are not.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Register your business and obtain the required environmental and local permits before buying your first vehicle.
  2. â Secure a site in an industrial or commercial zone, with hard standing, drainage control, and room for expansion.
  3. â Buy core tools first â grinder, socket set, jack, drain pans, and a scale. Add specialised equipment as revenue grows.
  4. â Equip every worker with boots, gloves, eye protection, ear protection, and a hi-vis vest.
  5. â Set up a first aid kit and train all staff on emergency procedures and battery acid first aid.
  6. â Never accept a vehicle without proof of ownership and a signed purchase record.
  7. â Store all fluids in labelled, sealed containers and use a licensed disposal contractor.
  8. â Record every transaction the same day â purchases, parts sales, metal sales, and cash balance.

Further Reading

  • Basel Convention â Technical Guidelines on End-of-Life Vehicles (UNEP)
  • Kenya National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) â EIA & Licensing
  • Nigeria NESREA â Environmental Permits & Regulations
  • South Africa Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) â Waste & ELV Guidelines
  • African Circular Economy Alliance â Automotive & Metals Sector Reports

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills programme. Always verify local regulations with the relevant authority before starting operations.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the car breaking value chain?
quiz.explanation: The value chain begins with sourcing old cars from individuals, insurers, or auctions.

quiz.q: In Africa, what is a typical price range for a non-running sedan?
quiz.explanation: A non-running sedan often costs between $200 and $500 depending on location and condition.

quiz.q: Which metal sells for $2â$4 per kilogram when recovered from cars?
quiz.explanation: Copper wiring and components are high-value and sell for $2â$4 per kg to foundries or exporters.

quiz.q: What is a common price for a tonne of mixed steel scrap in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Mixed steel scrap typically earns $150â$300 per tonne depending on market and country.

quiz.q: Why is separating metals important?
options: A) It makes the yard look tidy
B) Contaminated loads get lower prices
D) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Buyers pay less for mixed or contaminated metal, so sorting increases your revenue.

quiz.q: Which document is essential for business registration in most African countries?
quiz.explanation: A business registration certificate from the companies commission is a basic legal requirement.

quiz.q: What does NEMA stand for in Kenya?
options: C) National Export and Manufacturing Agency
D) National Energy and Mining Authority
quiz.explanation: NEMA is the National Environment Management Authority, which requires an EIA for larger yards.

quiz.q: Why is a police clearance certificate sometimes required for scrap dealers?
options: A) To prove you have no criminal record
B) To prove you are not dealing in stolen vehicles
C) To get a tax rebate
quiz.explanation: Police clearance helps ensure the dealer is not handling stolen vehicles or parts.

quiz.q: What should you keep for every car you buy?
options: B) Receipt, seller's ID copy, and vehicle papers
C) A photo of the car
quiz.explanation: Keeping receipts, seller ID, and vehicle papers protects you from legal issues.

quiz.q: Why is open burning of cables illegal in many African countries?
quiz.explanation: Burning cables releases harmful toxins and is banned to protect health and environment.

quiz.q: What is an ideal location for a scrapyard?
options: B) On the outskirts of town along a major road
quiz.explanation: Outskirts along major roads offer accessibility, space, and less disturbance to residents.

quiz.q: How much land is recommended to start a scrapyard?
options: C) At least half an acre (2,000 sq m)
quiz.explanation: At least half an acre gives enough space for vehicles, dismantling, and metal storage.

quiz.q: Why is a site near a mechanic village beneficial?
options: B) Ready supply of old cars and buyers for parts
quiz.explanation: Mechanic villages provide both a source of end-of-life vehicles and customers for used parts.

quiz.q: What should you check before renting land for a scrapyard?
options: B) The colour of the soil
D) Distance to the nearest bar
quiz.explanation: Zoning laws determine whether you can legally operate an industrial scrapyard on that land.

quiz.q: Why is a written lease important?
options: B) It prevents eviction and protects your investment
D) It is required by police
quiz.explanation: A written lease of 3â5 years gives security and prevents sudden eviction.

quiz.q: Which hand tool is essential for removing wheels?
quiz.explanation: A wheel brace (or lug wrench) is needed to loosen and remove wheel nuts.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a good socket set?
quiz.explanation: A basic socket set of 8mmâ24mm costs around $30â$60.

quiz.q: Which power tool is most versatile for cutting metal in a scrapyard?
quiz.explanation: An angle grinder with cutting and grinding discs can cut exhausts, chassis, and seized bolts.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a torque wrench?
options: B) To tighten bolts to a specific tension
quiz.explanation: A torque wrench ensures bolts are tightened to the manufacturer's specified torque, preventing damage.

quiz.q: Why is a fire extinguisher necessary in a scrapyard?
options: A) To put out fuel or electrical fires
quiz.explanation: Scrapyards have flammable fluids and materials, so a fire extinguisher is essential for safety.

quiz.q: What should you wear when grinding metal?
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses and gloves protect against flying metal fragments and cuts.

quiz.q: How should you treat a deep cut with heavy bleeding?
options: B) Apply pressure and seek medical help
quiz.explanation: Applying direct pressure helps stop bleeding; then get professional medical attention.

quiz.q: What is the correct first aid for a burn?
options: B) Cool with running water for 10 minutes
quiz.explanation: Cooling a burn with running water reduces damage and pain; then cover loosely.

quiz.q: How should you handle used oil?
options: A) Pour it on the ground
B) Drain into labelled containers for recycling
quiz.explanation: Used oil must be collected in labelled containers and sold to recyclers, not dumped or burned.

quiz.q: What should you do if battery acid spills?
quiz.explanation: Baking soda neutralises battery acid safely; then clean up according to safety procedures.

quiz.q: What is the simplest record-keeping tool for a beginner?
quiz.explanation: A simple cash book notebook with columns for date, description, money in, and money out is easy and cheap.

quiz.q: Why should you record the seller's ID and vehicle papers when buying a car?
options: B) To prove the car is not stolen
quiz.explanation: Keeping seller ID and vehicle papers protects you from accusations of dealing in stolen goods.

quiz.q: What should you do at the end of each week with your records?
quiz.explanation: Weekly totals help you track profit and make informed business decisions.

quiz.q: Why is an inventory list important?
options: A) It prevents theft and helps answer customers
B) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: An up-to-date inventory helps you know what you have, prevents theft, and speeds up sales.

quiz.q: How can you use a smartphone for record keeping?
options: A) Use a free spreadsheet app like Google Sheets
quiz.explanation: A free spreadsheet app can serve as a digital cash book and inventory list.
